Vero Beach Recreation Department will present 2016 Takeover, the 52nd Aerial Antics Youth Circus, at St. Edwards School, 1895 Saint Edwards Drive, Vero Beach on Thursday, July 30, Friday, July 31 and Saturday, Aug. 1. Tickets cost $8 for adults, $7 for children and seniors, and are free to children under 5.

The annual youth circus marks its 52nd year of performances in Vero Beach. Community members can purchase tickets and attend any of the three performance dates at St. Edwards School. More information is available by calling 772-770-6500 or 772-978-4500.

cards.headline: Environmental Learning Center offers multiple summer programs in Vero Beach
cards.teaser: The Environmental Learning Center at 255 Live Oak Drive in Vero Beach is hosting several summer programs including a back-to-school ice cream social, family paddle classes and art workshops.
cards.body:
The Environmental Learning Center, 255 Live Oak Drive, Vero Beach is hosting multiple summer programs throughout August. Cook Connect: Cooking Up Family Memories with Chef Stacy Maple, a Back to School Ice Cream Social, will take place Saturday, Aug. 8. A Family Paddle Pro Class is scheduled for Saturday, Aug. 15, from 1:30 to 3:30 p.m., costing $35 for adults and free to children under 18 with a participating adult.

Additional programs include a BYOB Sip Paint event on Friday, Aug. 21, and a Nourish Flourish: Knife Skills class with Chef Stacy Maple on Saturday, Aug. 22, costing $20 for ages 12 and older. Community members can register for programs and find more information at discoverelc.org.

cards.headline: Boca Raton TLC Program Offers Summer Service Projects for South Florida Families
cards.teaser: B'nai Torah Congregation's TLC Program connects volunteers with hands-on service projects ranging from food support and shoe donations to pantry stocking and literacy efforts.
cards.body:
B'nai Torah Congregation's TLC Program is offering South Florida families a range of hands-on service projects this summer, from food support and shoe donations to pantry stocking, literacy efforts and care for seniors. Led by Summer Faerman, the program connects volunteers of all ages with mitzvah opportunities, or meaningful good deeds, as part of the congregation's broader community outreach efforts.

 The TLC Program stands for Tzedakah, Learning and Chesed, and has made service a central part of synagogue life since 2012. The program provides a way for individuals and families to put Jewish values into action while helping people in need across South Florida. It addresses multiple community concerns including hunger, homelessness, literacy, elder care, vulnerable populations and special needs. Organizers emphasize that the projects are open to everyone in the community, not only members of B'nai Torah Congregation, with the goal of making service practical, welcoming and easy to begin.

 Participants can volunteer in various ways throughout the summer. Projects include making sandwiches, serving meals, collecting and cleaning shoes, stocking Little Free Pantries, preparing backpacks for back-to-school efforts, creating Bags of Hope and helping seniors with technology. Organizers plan to demonstrate volunteer projects such as wrapping presents, making flower arrangements, preparing sandwiches, collecting shoes and assembling supplies for people in need. The variety of options allows families to choose activities that match their interests and schedules.

 As summer continues, the TLC Program offers families a way to stay connected, teach children about giving back and support neighbors throughout South Florida. B'nai Torah Congregation says the program is built around the idea that small acts of service can strengthen the larger community. More information about the TLC Program is available through B'nai Torah Congregation's website.

hero.headline: Judge rules James Fishback can remain on Florida governor ballot after residency challenge
hero.body:
Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback will remain on Florida's Aug. 18 primary ballot after Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank rejected Lt. Gov. Jay Collins' challenge to his residency qualifications. Frank ruled Monday that Collins did not present enough evidence to overcome Florida's legal presumptions favoring continued residency and candidate access to the ballot. The judge wrote that the court will not be deciding the race between the lieutenant governor and Fishback, adding that decision will be in the sound hands of the voters. The final order denies Collins' request to remove Fishback, declares that the Department of State properly certified his candidacy and says Fishback shall remain qualified for the Republican nomination for governor.

Collins sued Fishback in June, arguing the candidate failed to meet the Florida Constitution's requirement that a governor reside in the state for the seven years preceding the election. During an expedited hearing last week, Collins' attorneys presented voter registration, mortgage, tax and homestead records they argued showed Fishback established legal residency in Washington, D.C., between 2019 and 2022. Fishback voted in Washington during the 2020 presidential election, filed D.C. resident income tax returns and signed mortgage paperwork describing a condominium there as his principal residence. Property tax records also showed the condominium received a D.C. homestead deduction. A forensic document examiner testified it was probable Fishback signed the disputed voter registration form.

Frank acknowledged those records could carry consequences outside the Florida candidacy case, writing that it may be true the various election and financial filings could result in regulatory, maybe even more severe legal, repercussions for Fishback under Washington, D.C. law. But the judge found they did not prove Fishback intended to abandon Florida as his permanent home. Fishback testified for several hours that he never intended to move his legal domicile from Florida. He acknowledged signing mortgage paperwork identifying the Washington condominium as his primary residence but said he rushed through the documents without reading them closely. He also characterized his 2020 D.C. vote as an inadvertent registration during the pandemic, saying he was staying with his parents and wanted to vote for President Donald Trump. Frank found Fishback credible on the central issue of intent, stating that despite defendant stating at various points his residence was in Washington, D.C., defendant never had an actual subjective intent to move his permanent residency from Florida.

Fishback's campaign called the ruling a victory for the Constitution and for every Floridian who believes elections should be decided by voters. Collins' attorney Mark Meuser criticized the ruling and argued the court improperly accepted Fishback's explanation that he did not understand the legal significance of his Washington filings. Meuser did not indicate whether Collins plans to appeal the ruling. Unless an appellate court intervenes, Fishback will remain on the Aug. 18 Republican primary ballot alongside Collins, U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds and former House Speaker Paul Renner.

cards.headline: Florida families say Medicaid abruptly stopped covering autism therapy without explanation
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County parents say their children lost access to Applied Behavioral Analysis after Medicaid stopped covering the therapy. Florida's health agency has not explained why.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County parents say their children lost access to Applied Behavioral Analysis after Medicaid abruptly stopped covering it. The Cleveland Clinic describes ABA as a research based behavior therapy for people with autism and other developmental disorders, adding that many studies have proven the effectiveness of ABA. Families connected to Reflection Services ABA Therapy in Lake Worth say they received notice that Medicaid would no longer cover their children's treatment. Daura Mabel Sanchez Cano de Fundora said her son David is classified by his neurologist as level one on the autism spectrum. She described how his vocabulary has been increasingly amazing and he can understand what is happening. Myrian Suarez, a mother of two boys with autism, said ABA gave her son tools to manage his emotions.

Since the therapy stopped, families described dangerous regressions in their children's behavior. Talia Quiroz said she has bites all over her body. Suarez described bruised arms from her son's pinching. Melissa Moran, a registered behavior technician at Reflection Services ABA Therapy, acknowledged the cost of the services but warned of societal repercussions. She said parents may not go to work, affecting the economy, and that some kids have unsafe behaviors including physical aggression and self injurious behaviors that may put themselves and other kids at risk.

Reports of Medicaid cuts to ABA therapy have surfaced in states across the country. The Health and Human Services Office of the Inspector General audited Medicaid spending on ABA in Maine, Michigan, Wisconsin and Colorado, identifying roughly $197.9 million in what it considers improper payments among the four states. A separate audit in Nebraska found yearly Medicaid spending on ABA therapy multiplied 18 times over across a five year period. U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr. said during a news conference last week that the administration is not sending Medicaid and Medicare dollars out the door until it has confidence they are being spent lawfully and appropriately.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds challenges David Jolly to Florida governor debates before primary concludes
cards.teaser: Republican front runner Byron Donalds challenged leading Democratic candidate David Jolly to three general election debates this fall, even as Donalds continues facing three opponents for the GOP nomination.
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial front runner Byron Donalds challenged leading Democratic candidate David Jolly to three general election debates this fall with less than a month remaining before Florida's Aug. 18 primary. Donalds continues facing three opponents for the GOP nomination. Donalds said when the time comes for these debates, his vision is one for a free Florida that puts the people of Florida first, protects the Florida dream, expands Florida's economies and makes sure Florida remains number one in all of America. Jolly, a former Republican congressman now running as a Democrat, initially responded by telling Donalds to survive his own primary first. During a later CNN appearance, however, he said he would gladly meet Donalds on the debate stage a dozen times, adding that Donalds should get through his Republican primary first.

The exchange gave Donalds' Republican opponents another opportunity to criticize the front runner for looking beyond them. Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner and businessman James Fishback have not received debate invitations from Donalds. Donalds has not debated his primary rivals while maintaining sizable advantages in polling, fundraising and endorsements. A recent Cygnal survey showed Donalds at 43 percent, compared with 12 percent for Fishback, 11 percent for Collins and 2 percent for Renner, although nearly one third of voters remained undecided.

A separate University of North Florida poll offered an early look at the possible general election matchup. Donalds led Jolly 46 percent to 41 percent among likely midterm voters, with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points. The poll surveyed 848 likely midterm voters from July 8 through July 17.

cards.headline: Poll shows Florida property tax amendment support drops after voters learn of budget impact
cards.teaser: A University of North Florida poll found 61 percent initial support for Florida's proposed property tax amendment. Support fell to 45 percent after respondents were told the proposal is estimated to create an approximately $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall over two years.
cards.body:
A new poll showed Florida's proposed property tax amendment may be popular enough to pass depending on how it is described to voters. The proposal would raise the homestead exemption for non school property taxes from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. It would also lower the annual assessment growth cap for non homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent and restrict how local governments spend remaining property tax revenue. The University of North Florida survey initially found 61 percent support after respondents were told the amendment would reserve property tax revenue for core public services. That is narrowly above the 60 percent approval required for a constitutional amendment.

Support fell 16 points after respondents were told the proposal is estimated to create an approximately $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall over two years. With that information, 45 percent supported the amendment and 47 percent opposed it. The poll surveyed 848 likely midterm voters from July 8 through July 17. Those results add significance to three lawsuits challenging the amendment's ballot title and summary. Plaintiffs argue phrases promising to protect small businesses, ensure fairness and preserve core services amount to political advertising instead of a neutral description of the proposal.

The challengers are not asking a judge to remove the amendment from the November ballot. If the language is found defective, state law would require Attorney General James Uthmeier to rewrite what voters see. A hearing on the ballot language challenges is scheduled for July 29 in Leon County. The cases could be consolidated ahead of that hearing.

cards.headline: Gov. Ron DeSantis secures Relativity Space expansion at Cape Canaveral during UK trade mission
cards.teaser: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis announced during a state business development mission through England and Scotland that Relativity Space plans to expand its operations at Cape Canaveral. The company plans an additional production facility for its Terran R rocket.
cards.body:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis led a state business development mission through England and Scotland this week, opening Florida's pavilion at the Farnborough International Airshow and announcing that Relativity Space plans to expand its operations at Cape Canaveral. The company plans an additional production facility for its Terran R rocket, along with expanded testing and launch infrastructure at Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. State officials say the project could create thousands of jobs by 2034. Relativity Space is also eligible for up to $134 million through Florida's Spaceport Improvement Program. DeSantis separately oversaw a cooperation agreement between Space Florida and the U.K. Space Agency aimed at research, innovation and commercial development.

In London, DeSantis and Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky met with leaders from Lloyd's of London and other insurance and reinsurance firms. The trip comes as Florida officials continue trying to attract additional private capital to the state's property insurance market. Officials said the meetings also explored a potential research partnership between Florida and the Lloyd's Lab insurance technology program.

The mission also produced new academic agreements. Florida International University and Scotland's Heriot Watt University agreed to pursue cooperation centered on free markets, political economy and the work of Adam Smith. The University of Florida and the University of St. Andrews established a broader framework for joint research and faculty and student exchanges in fields including quantum, marine and physical sciences.

cards.headline: Boston cyclist rides 2,600 miles from Key West to Maine to honor friend lost to colorectal cancer
cards.teaser: Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin a 2,600 mile bike ride from Key West to Maine, with a goal of raising $50,000 for research while honoring his friend's memory.
cards.body:
Boston cyclist Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin a 2,600 mile bike ride from Key West to Maine after losing a close friend to young onset colorectal cancer. Weedall said a friend of his recently passed away from young onset rectal cancer. The death of his friend, who was also named Jay, inspired Weedall to honor his memory by riding his bike across the country. Weedall said he has adventured around the world with his friend, ridden bikes together with him, and this felt like the best way to honor him now that he has passed away. His goal is to raise $50,000 for the Young Onset Colorectal Cancer Research Center in honor of the friend he lost to the disease. To prepare, Weedall trained 200 to 300 miles a week, mapped out his route and planned for the long journey ahead.

Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on day one. He set off on his second leg a 163 mile ride to Vero Beach. Weedall said he tries to beat the heat and is going roughly 150 miles a day just niching his way up the coast through pretty much every state all the way to the Pan Mass Challenge. He will do the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2 and continue to the Canadian border in Maine. By avoiding highways, Weedall says the route offers something unexpected, allowing him to experience little coastal towns along the inlets.

Weedall said even when his legs are hurting, even when the traffic is big or even when he is a little anxious about what is going on around him, he is largely just thinking about his friend who does not get the opportunity to do this with him anymore. Fans can follow Weedall's journey on the cycling app Strava.

cards.headline: Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach showcases medical breakthroughs from ancient sea creatures
cards.teaser: Researchers at the Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach have developed an antidote for the potentially fatal sting of the box jellyfish. Other medical advances include collagen harvested from flame jellies that has been found to help stop hemorrhages.
cards.body:
The Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach houses thousands of jellyfish in all sizes and shapes, offering a window into some of the ocean's most ethereal and elusive creatures. Naphtalie Jeanty, who holds degrees in both archaeology and anthropology, found her way to the museum through a passion for teaching about flora and fauna. Jellyfish have been gracefully moving through the world's oceans for over 500 million years, making them some of the oldest living species on Earth, predating dinosaurs, trees and even fish. Despite the name, jellyfish are not technically fish at all. Jeanty said a lot of the world is starting to describe them as just jellies, and they do not have the same anatomy as fish.

Researchers at the museum have developed an antidote for the potentially fatal sting of the box jellyfish, which can kill its prey in 3 to 5 minutes. Jeanty said she thinks it is going to be a breakthrough. Other medical advances involve collagen harvested from flame jellies. The collagen has been apparently found to help stop hemorrhages, so it might be found in bandages in the future. Research into the Japanese sea nettle has also yielded promising results. There is a part of them that was found to shrink tumors in a mouse cancer, and the next step would be possibly human cancer.

Jellyfish also perform something called symmetrization, the ability to reorganize their bodies for balance. Moon jellies can regenerate after being split in half, creating two different versions of themselves. Some jellyfish even scrub out microplastics, among the smallest particles of pollution found in seas. Polka dotted jellies on display at the museum are native to a lake on the island of Palau in the South Pacific, where they work to keep the lake alive. Jeanty said they provide nutrients and move nutrients all throughout the ocean, taking out excess ones that do not need to be there.

hero.headline: Indiantown Council rejects second attempt to pause data center applications
hero.body:
The Indiantown Village Council on Monday declined to implement a 90-day pause on data center applications despite renewed pressure from residents and two council members. Councilwoman Karen Onsager proposed the pause to allow time for the council to study infrastructure demands on water and electrical systems before making decisions on data center projects. She requested a community informational meeting with technical experts, representatives from the South Florida Water Management District, and utility providers before any votes on future applications.

Councilwoman Vernestine Palmer said she supported a longer pause of 12 to 18 months to gather information and update land development regulations with safeguards. Indiantown civic activist Melissa Hague told the council during the July 13 budget workshop that refusing to pause applications was negligent when officials admitted they did not fully understand data center impacts. Nelson Ferreira had submitted a data center application earlier this year but withdrew it on April 29 after scores of residents protested during preliminary review.

Village Attorney Wade Vose warned that any pause would violate Senate Bills 180 and 484 and expose the municipality to lawsuits from property owners and developers. Vose said a local land use attorney who represents multiple developers in the village emailed him the same afternoon warning that SB 180 prohibits any regulation that would inhibit development applications. Village Manager Taryn Kryzda confirmed that data centers are a permitted use on industrially zoned lands within the village.

Mayor Carmine Dipaolo warned that defying the Legislature could jeopardize state funding after Indiantown received over $120 million in recent years. Kryzda said local governments that go against state or federal government typically face withheld funding. Onsager's motion died after no council member offered a second. The community informational meeting Onsager requested will be held Saturday, Aug. 2.

cards.headline: Big Taste of Martin County returns to Stuart in October to support youth mentoring programs
cards.teaser: Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties will host the Big Taste of Martin County on Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together
cards.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties will host the Big Taste of Martin County on Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

 Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

 Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties said the event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. The nonprofit serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.

 Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

cards.headline: Treasure Coast single-family home prices rise after two-year decline
cards.teaser: Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St.
cards.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

 Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

 Cara Collins, who bought her Martin County home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said current prices are higher than she would hope for, and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. She said she would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and be able to afford a home for her kids if buying now.

 Condos and townhomes show different trends. Prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County. Decowski said buyers need to come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes, and sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue faces $16.5M loss, 116 job cuts if property tax reform passes
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose $16.5 million if voters approve property tax reform in November, according to public records. County commissioners are set to discuss what thos
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue could lose $16.5 million if voters approve property tax reform in November, according to public records. County commissioners are set to discuss what those changes could mean for the fire department in a commission meeting Tuesday. The proposed reform would increase the homestead exemption over two years, and the department is bracing for the impact.

 Rick Sterl, president of the Martin County Firefighters Association, IAFF Local 2959, said most of the department's funding comes from ad-valorem and general fund revenue. If voters approve the reform, Martin County Fire Rescue's presentation outlines two stark options: cut services or cut staff. Cutting services would mean closing fire stations, ending hazmat, dive and technical rescue operations, grounding the critical care helicopter, and using firefighting equipment past its lifespan. Cutting staff would mean eliminating 116 firefighters over two years, roughly one in three firefighters in the department.

 Sterl said the consequences of either path would be felt by the public. "Any reductions is going to possibly change the outcome of the level of care the response time," said Sterl. "At the end of the day, any cuts is someone is going to pay the price." According to public records, both options create compounding problems.

 Cut services and remaining personnel can't respond properly, or cut firefighters and there won't be enough staff to maintain existing services. Fire rescue argues no version of the proposal allows the department to remain whole.

 Residents in Martin County offered mixed reactions to the potential cuts. Joe Vessichio said he doesn't believe the cuts will happen. "Neither one is going to happen, we have more than enough money," said Vessichio.

 "And even if it does, big deal, so a couple of people lose their job, they get retrained to do something else." Lisa Freitas, owner of Lisa Gay Fashions, expressed concern about what cuts could mean for public safety. "Wow, what a job they do. You can't go that route for our safety. They protect our families," said Freitas.

cards.headline: Martin and St. Lucie counties report five confirmed cases of cyclosporiasiasis
cards.teaser: The Florida Department of Health has confirmed 94 cases of cyclosporiasiasis statewide, including two in St. Lucie County, two in Palm Beach County and one in Martin County.
cards.body:
Growing outbreaks linked to bacteria and parasites on produce continue making headlines. The Florida Department of Health has confirmed 94 cases of cyclosporiasis statewide, including two in Palm Beach County, two in St. Lucie County and one in Martin County.

 Ryan Boylston of Delray Beach has responded by growing his own produce in his front yard. His property includes spinach, lettuce, arugula, star fruit, bananas, peppers, pineapple and herbs that his family eats every day. Boylston started growing his own food about three years ago after struggling to find produce he felt was healthy and free of chemicals or contaminants.

 He now helps others install gardens in their own yards through his company, Urban Abundance. The other half of his property is filled with herbs and vegetables growing in raised planters similar to the ones he builds for customers. For beginners interested in starting their own garden, Boylston recommends growing crops that can handle Florida's summer heat, including spinach, sweet potatoes and yardlong beans.

 He says lettuce and tomatoes do much better during the winter months. Boylston recommends raised garden beds with smooth sides that iguanas cannot easily climb, and suggests building cages or enclosures around plants growing directly in the ground for protection.

cards.headline: Palm City dog trainer trial delayed for eighth time as judge voices frustration in Martin County court
cards.teaser: Tempers flared in a Martin County courtroom Tuesday as Judge Elizabeth Metzger pressed both prosecution and defense over why the animal cruelty case against Nikki Camerlengo still hasn't gone to trial more than two years after charges were filed.
cards.body:
The hearing marked the eighth continuance in the case against Palm City dog trainer, groomer and boarder Nikki Camerlengo. Judge Elizabeth Metzger made her frustration clear from the bench, telling both legal teams the case has been continued so many times she has lost count. At one point, an exchange between the judge and Camerlengo's defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, grew heated. When Kaplan said the delays were of no fault of the defendant, Metzger replied "I'm not saying that!" as Kaplan protested "You're looking at me!"

 Camerlengo was arrested in 2024 on two felony animal cruelty charges after Martin County detectives said two dogs died in her care. The arrest followed a WPTV investigation by Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to Camerlengo's Pawsitively Paradise facility over the course of a decade. Kaplan is asking the court to block testimony from both the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed the two necropsies and from lead investigator Detective Christine Polizzi.

 Prosecutor Kristen Chase did not oppose the latest continuance, saying she is waiting on a deposition of her expert witness scheduled for July 31, delayed by scheduling conflicts. Another status hearing is set for Aug. 3, after the expert deposition.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Police open $28.8 million training facility with indoor firearms range
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie Police cut the ribbon on a three-story, 54,283-square-foot training center on the City Hall grounds after four years of construction.
cards.body:
The new police training center officially opened on July 24 with a ribbon-cutting attended by Mayor Shannon Martin and Chief Leo Niemczyk. The facility includes a 20-lane, 9,508-square-foot indoor firearms range featuring an integrated MILO live-fire scenario system, a 2,848-square-foot tactical shoot house with configurable rooms, and a MILO Virtual Simulation Theater for decision-making and de-escalation exercises.

The three-story building houses a defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology, a multi-purpose training room for classroom instruction, and three floors of office space supporting the Training Division and Criminal Investigations Division with 19 offices and 86 workstations. The facility was designed by ADG Architecture and constructed by HJ High.

Officer Brittany McNally said that for years, officers traveled to Indian River State College in Fort Pierce for extensive training. By bringing training in-house, the facility will reduce recurring costs while allowing officers to train more efficiently. Police personnel immediately began moving into the new facility after the ribbon cutting.

cards.headline: Armed robbery at Fort Pierce Wells Fargo ATM forces victim to withdraw cash
cards.teaser: Two men forced a victim to withdraw cash at gunpoint at a Wells Fargo ATM on Sunday evening before fleeing on foot.
cards.body:
The Fort Pierce Police Department said the robbery happened Sunday at about 8:38 p.m. when two men approached a victim using the ATM. One of the men displayed a gun concealed in his waistband before forcing the victim to withdraw an unknown amount of cash.

Officers responded to the scene, established a perimeter, and used a K-9 and drone to search for the suspects. The suspects were not located. Police described them as two men in their early 20s, about 5 feet 10 inches tall and weighing about 170 pounds. The armed suspect was last seen wearing jeans and a gray hooded sweatshirt.

cards.headline: Two suspects arrested after 80 mph chase in Port St. Lucie, one found hiding on roof
cards.teaser: A driver fled police at nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone on Southwest Becker Road before abandoning the vehicle and fleeing on foot with a passenger.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie Police attempted to stop a white Acura after observing multiple traffic violations and signs of impaired driving. The driver accelerated to nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone on Southwest Becker Road, weaving in and out of traffic and ignoring traffic signs and signals. The driver and passenger abandoned the vehicle in a residential driveway near Southwest Idol Avenue before fleeing on foot.

A nearby resident called 911 after seeing the two men run from the scene. Police deployed a K-9 and a drone while officers established a perimeter. Both suspects were located, including one who was found hiding on the roof of an occupied home.

The suspects were identified as Joseph Gary Harris, 42, and Bryan Shawn Baker, 46. Harris was charged with fleeing and eluding law enforcement, burglary of an occupied dwelling, resisting an officer without violence, and loitering or prowling. Baker was charged with resisting an officer without violence and loitering or prowling.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County corrections deputy sentenced to probation after road rage incident
cards.teaser: Devin Mills, 57, was sentenced to two years of probation after pleading no contest to burglary of a conveyance charge related to an off-duty incident on Southwest Tulip Boulevard in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
According to court documents in St. Lucie County, Mills was sentenced on Thursday, July 16, to two years of probation and must pay court costs. He pleaded no contest to burglary of a conveyance charge on June 29. Florida Department of Corrections database records indicate Mills' probation is supervised by its Fort Pierce Circuit office and expires on July 15, 2028.

Court documents note Mills' probation will automatically terminate after one year if he completes conditions of probation, which include a mental health evaluation and if needed, treatment, along with no contact with the victims or victims' families during the probation. Mills was accused of confronting two 18-year-olds in a vehicle during a road rage incident on the 100 block of Southwest Tulip Boulevard in Port St. Lucie. A video recording by the teenagers showed Mills reaching into the open passenger side of the teens' vehicle, grabbing one of the teens' arms to take the cellphone that was recording the incident away.

After his no-contest plea, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said Mills remained on unpaid administrative leave pending an internal investigation. A spokesperson for the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said on Thursday, July 23 that Mills' employment status is pending the completion of an internal affairs investigation.

cards.headline: P1 Motor Club building private racetrack resort on 650 acres in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: The new private racetrack resort community is under construction on 650 acres off Okeechobee Road, featuring 10 miles of racing circuits and set to welcome its first drivers this fall.
cards.body:
P1 Motor Club is designed for drivers of all ages and skill levels, with tracks for street cars, race cars, and go-karts. Chris DuPlessis, Director of Fun for P1 Motor Club, said kids as young as 8 years old can drive go-karts. The first track under construction is the 3-mile Treasure Coast Track, set to open in October. Over the next six months, crews will continue work on additional circuits, including the flagship 4.5-mile P1 International Circuit.

Membership comes with a $192,000 initiation fee and $12,000 in yearly dues. The club already has 260 members. Construction on a clubhouse and homes for up to 125 residents is scheduled to begin in 2027. The development will also include condos and customizable garages with living spaces situated directly along the tracks.

Developers say they want to preserve the character of the region by planting trees, creating lakes, and incorporating natural landscaping throughout the property. P1 Motor Club is expected to be fully completed by 2028.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Police Unveil New $28 Million Training Facility
cards.teaser: The 54,283-square-foot facility includes an indoor firearms range, tactical shoot house, virtual simulation theater and dedicated training spaces for Port St. Lucie police.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie Police Department has unveiled a new $28 million training facility designed to provide officers with updated technology and specialized spaces for law enforcement instruction.

 The department held a ribbon-cutting ceremony Friday, giving members of the media a first look inside the 54,283-square-foot building before it becomes operational.

 Facility includes range, tactical and simulation training

 The new facility includes a 20-lane indoor firearms range and a tactical shoot house where officers can participate in scenario-based exercises.

 A MILO virtual simulation theater will be used for decision-making and de-escalation training, while a defensive tactics room is equipped with Axon virtual reality technology.

 The building also features a multi-purpose training room, updated audio and visual systems, and office space for the department's Training Division and Criminal Investigations Division.

 Police cite city's continued growth

 Port St. Lucie police said the facility was developed to support the department's continuing training needs as the city grows.

 The project was designed by ADG Architecture and constructed by HJ High. Specialized equipment and technology were provided by companies including Action Target, MILO and Whelen.

 Department personnel are expected to begin moving into the building Saturday, July 25.

 Police said the secure training facility will not be open to the public.

The ride honors his close friend, also named Jay, who recently died from young-onset rectal cancer. The two had adventured around the world together and ridden bikes together.

cards.headline: Indian River County firefighter Geoffrey Lang dies following personal tragedy at Sebastian home
cards.teaser: Indian River County Fire Rescue is mourning the loss of Firefighter/Paramedic Geoffrey Lang, who died Saturday following what officials described as a personal .
cards.body:
Indian River County Fire Rescue is mourning the loss of Firefighter/Paramedic Geoffrey Lang, who died Saturday following what officials described as a personal tragedy at his Sebastian home. Lang was 35 years old and is survived by his wife, two children and his parents.

Lang joined Indian River County Fire Rescue in 2015 and served the community for more than a decade. He worked out of Station 9 at 13550 Roseland Road in Sebastian. County officials said he was known for his professionalism, compassion and dedication to serving others.

Fire Chief David Johnson said Lang's absence will be deeply felt throughout the department. County Administrator John A. said the county's thoughts are with Lang's family, friends and fellow firefighters during this difficult time. County Commission Chairman Deryl Loar extended condolences on behalf of the Board of County Commissioners and emphasized the county's commitment to supporting the mental health and well-being of first responders and their families.

Indian River County Fire Rescue asked the public to respect the privacy of Lang's family, friends and colleagues as they grieve. Officials said memorial service information will be released when it becomes available. Multiple agencies across Indian River County, including the Sebastian Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department and Indian River County Sheriff's Office, expressed condolences to Lang's family and colleagues.

cards.headline: Sebastian Police Department mourns death of Indian River County firefighter
cards.teaser: Sebastian Police Department and multiple Treasure Coast law enforcement agencies expressed condolences following the death of Firefighter Geoffrey Lang.
cards.body:
The Sebastian Police Department joined Indian River County Fire Rescue in mourning the loss of Firefighter Geoffrey Lang, who died while off duty Saturday night. The department said Lang's bravery and service will always be remembered and extended deepest condolences to his family, friends and fellow firefighters.
